content: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is an RNA virus that primarily infects plants, particularly tobacco and other members of the Solanaceae family. It causes characteristic symptoms such as mottling and discoloration on the leaves, which is the origin of its name. TMV holds historical significance as the first virus ever discovered. Although the disease affecting tobacco crops was recognized in the late 19th century, it was not until 1930 that the causative agent was identified as a virus. In 1883, Adolf Mayer first described the disease and demonstrated that it could be transmitted between plants, resembling bacterial infections. However, in 1889, Martinus Beijerinck provided evidence that a filtered, bacteria-free culture medium still contained the infectious agent, which he termed a contagium vivum fluidum (a contagious living fluid). Dimitri Ivanovski provided the first concrete evidence of the virus's existence in 1892. In 1935, Wendell Meredith Stanley successfully crystallized the virus, enabling its study under electron microscopy. Remarkably, he demonstrated that the virus remained biologically active even after crystallization. For this groundbreaking work, Stanley was awarded one-quarter of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1946. In 1955, Heinz Fraenkel-Conrat and Robley Williams demonstrated that purified TMV RNA and its capsid protein could spontaneously assemble into functional viruses. This finding suggested that the assembled structure represents the most stable configuration, with the lowest free energy, and likely reflects the natural assembly process within host cells. Rosalind Franklin, a renowned crystallographer, briefly worked with Stanley at Berkeley and later constructed a model of TMV for the 1958 World's Fair in Brussels. In the same year, she hypothesized that the virus was hollow rather than solid and proposed that TMV RNA is single-stranded. This hypothesis was later confirmed posthumously, and it is now known that TMV RNA is a positive-sense (+) strand. Structurally, TMV has a rod-like appearance. Its capsid is composed of 2,130 identical coat protein molecules and a single molecule of genomic RNA, which is 6,390 bases in length. The coat protein self-assembles into a helical rod-like structure, with 16.3 protein subunits per helical turn, surrounding the RNA. The RNA itself forms a hairpin loop structure. Each protein monomer consists of 158 amino acids, organized into four primary alpha-helices connected by a prominent loop near the virion's axis. The virions are approximately 300 nanometers in length and 18 nanometers in diameter. Electron micrographs, using negative staining, reveal a distinct inner channel approximately 4 nanometers in diameter. The RNA is located at a radius of about 6 nanometers and is protected from enzymatic degradation by the surrounding coat protein. Each protein monomer interacts with three RNA nucleotides. TMV has significant scientific and environmental implications. In plants, it causes substantial crop losses, infecting members of nine plant families and at least 125 individual species, including economically important crops such as tobacco, tomato, pepper, and cucumbers, as well as various ornamental flowers. Numerous strains of TMV exist. The virus has been extensively studied in structural molecular biology, X-ray diffraction, and virus assembly and disassembly due to its unique properties. TMV is particularly advantageous for research because it can be produced in large quantities and does not infect animals. By cultivating a few infected tobacco plants in a greenhouse and performing simple laboratory procedures, researchers can easily obtain several grams of the virus. This ease of production allows TMV to be treated almost like an organic chemical rather than a conventional infectious agent.
